articles.title: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.summary: In a speech overlooking the Acropolis, the US Secretary of State also said the US believes Europe "can awaken from its long slumber".
articles.body:
Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline.

Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together".

"We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said.

While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests".

Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers.

But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads.

"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century."

Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation".

That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world".

"The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.

"In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay."

Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships.

Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence.

Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal.

articles.title: In 2024, Texas’ largest wildfire burned about 46,000 acres of the 77,721-acre Turkey Track Ranch; after rebuilding 65 miles of fencing, its owners have put it back on the market for $180 million
articles.summary: Turkey Track Ranch, a historic Texas Panhandle property spanning 77,721 acres, is back on the market, asking $180 million after recovering from the
articles.body: Turkey Track Ranch, a historic Texas Panhandle property spanning 77,721 acres, is back on the market, asking $180 million after recovering from the devastating Smokehouse Creek Fire of February 2024.The ranch, which stretches from the Caprock country to the Canadian River, was already up for sale when the wildfire swept through it. The fire burned about 60% of its rangeland, so the owners took it off the market and gave the land time to recover.Now, with vegetation and wildlife returning, 65 miles of new fencing installed and the cattle operation running again, the owners have decided to resume the sale.Getting caught in the largest wildfire in TexasThe Smokehouse Creek Fire was the largest wildfire in recorded Texas history, burning more than one million acres across the Texas Panhandle and into western Oklahoma.Over 46,000 acres of the Turkey Track Ranch were burned in the fire. It killed thousands of head of livestock, caused two human fatalities and destroyed about 500 buildings across the wider area. The fire began after a utility pole adjacent to the Turkey Track Ranch boundary fell and brought down live power lines.During the time of the fire, the owners were in sale negotiations. They withdrew the ranch from the market and gave the land time to recover. The land has come back with renewed strength and vigour, including robust regrowth of native vegetation, pastures and wildlife. New fencing has been installed across about 65 miles, and the cattle operation is again in full swing. The managers representing the ranch’s shareholders have now voted to put it back on the market and move ahead with the sale.Water is one of its biggest assetsBeyond its massive size, water is the biggest asset of the property. The ranch has approximately 26 miles of Canadian River frontage. Stretching from Caprock country to the Canadian River, the ranch includes high mesas, open range, sheltered draws and river bottoms. The property also has eight major creek basins and natural springs, with the Ogallala Aquifer beneath the land. There are 64 water wells that serve livestock and wildlife across the ranch. There are five irrigation pivots that cover 838 acres.Back in the 1950s, when drought struck, the family began building earthen dams to slow runoff and protect the soil. Over the decades, this conservation work continued. In 2016, Turkey Track was named a regional honouree of the Environmental Stewardship Award Program for its land and water management."I have represented some of the great ranches of the American West, and Turkey Track belongs in their company. The water here is extraordinary, the legacy and history incredible. It is a best-in-class and rarity both. Available legacy ranches with this scale, production, recreation and history are today few and far between, scarce anywhere in the American West. Nearly 80,000 acres under one fence, a 25 per cent mineral stake and more than a century of family ownership make this a very rare offering. This is a ranch you buy with the next hundred years in mind," Bernard Uechtritz, the founder of the real-estate brokerage handling the sale of Turkey Track Ranch, said.The ranch also includes the sites of the 1864 and 1874 Adobe Walls battles. Its brand dates back to 1878, while W. T. Coble acquired the original ranch headquarters in 1916. More than 100 years of Coble and Whittenburg family ownership have shaped the ranch. According to the brokerage firm, the 77,721-acre ranch is a rare opportunity to own a landmark of American ranching and shape its future for generations to come.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Texas ranchers blocked well operators from a 1,604-acre tract in 2004; on October 1, an appeals court ruled an oil company may cross the land to plug a shut-in well 15 to 20 yards from the San Antonio River
articles.summary: A long-running dispute between a South Texas ranch owner and an oil company over access to a shut-in well took another turn October 1, when a Texas
articles.body: A long-running dispute between a South Texas ranch owner and an oil company over access to a shut-in well took another turn October 1, when a Texas appeals court ruled that state law allows the operator to cross neighboring private land to reach the well for plugging work. The ruling came from the Texas Thirteenth Court of Appeals in Dierlam v. Allegiant Resources. The court affirmed a Victoria County trial court’s refusal to block the company’s access, according to the Texas Thirteenth Court of Appeals opinion published by Justia.The case involves a 1,604-acre tract in Victoria County that is part of the historic McFaddin Ranch. The ranch has deep roots in South Texas, with the Texas State Historical Association noting that James A. McFaddin began ranching in Victoria County in 1876. The area later became known as McFaddin Ranch and developed a long association with ranching in the region.At the heart of the dispute is the Remora Oil Unit No. 1, an oil and gas well located on neighboring property known as the Wright Land. Allegiant Resources and its predecessors operated the well from 1996 through 2015, according to the Texas appeals court opinion. The well has since been shut in, and Allegiant now wants to plug it rather than resume production. The problem is access.A 2004 injunction complicated accessThe ranch owner, Virginia L. Dierlam and McFaddin Ranch LP, obtained a permanent injunction in 2004 preventing well operators from using the ranch to reach the Remora well. That arrangement had nevertheless existed for years before the well was shut in. According to the appellate opinion, Allegiant’s predecessors paid more than $120,000 between 1996 and June 2015 for access to the ranch. Those payments stopped after the well became inactive.Allegiant became the operator in 2021 and later sought to negotiate new access with the ranch owners. The parties were unable to agree on financial terms, and access was ultimately refused. The company argued that it needed to reach the well because leaving it unplugged could create environmental and regulatory problems. The well is only about 15 to 20 yards from the San Antonio River, according to testimony described in the court’s opinion. Allegiant also told the trial court that it had considered several alternative routes but found that each would still require crossing the Dierlam property. One proposed route would involve clearing downed trees and low vegetation and was considered the least invasive option.Court says Texas law permits entryThe legal question before the appeals court was narrower than whether Allegiant could permanently establish an access easement across the ranch. Instead, the court considered whether the ranch owners were entitled to a temporary injunction preventing Allegiant from entering the property to plug the well. The answer was no.The court relied on Section 89.044 of the Texas Natural Resources Code, which permits the Railroad Commission, its agents, an operator or a nonoperator to enter “the land of another” to plug or replug a well that has not been properly plugged. The judges rejected the ranch owners’ argument that the provision applies only to land owned by the surface owner associated with the well itself. The court said the Legislature deliberately used the broader phrase “land of another” and did not restrict the access provision to a particular category of landowner. The decision also noted that the statute contains protections for surface owners, including provisions requiring restoration of land after plugging and limiting actions that could prevent the surface owner from accessing the property.Environmental concerns became centralAllegiant’s argument was not that it wanted to restart production at the Remora well. Its stated purpose was to plug the inactive well and remove the associated surface equipment. Company personnel told the trial court that an improperly abandoned well could potentially release saltwater or crude oil. They also raised concerns about deteriorating equipment and possible groundwater contamination.The company further argued that failing to complete the work could expose it to regulatory consequences from the Texas Railroad Commission and potentially significant financial losses. The appeals court did not ultimately decide all of those underlying environmental and financial questions. Its ruling focused on whether Dierlam had demonstrated a probable right to stop the access sought by Allegiant through a temporary injunction. It concluded that she had not.What the ruling does and does not meanThe October 1 decision does not amount to a final ruling resolving every aspect of the broader dispute between the ranch owners and Allegiant. The appellate court affirmed the trial court’s judgment denying Dierlam’s request for a temporary injunction. It also clarified that the trial court had not granted Allegiant’s separate request for a temporary injunction, despite arguments from Dierlam that it had effectively done so. The ruling instead establishes, at this stage of the litigation, that Section 89.044 gives Allegiant a statutory basis to enter the ranch for the limited purpose of plugging or replugging a well that has not been properly plugged.The case also highlights a broader tension in Texas oil country: private landowners’ rights can collide with the state’s regulatory authority over abandoned and inactive oil and gas wells, particularly when a well sits close to a waterway. For the McFaddin Ranch, the October ruling means the decades-old fight over access to the property now has a significant new chapter. The appellate court’s decision leaves Allegiant with a legal path to reach the shut-in Remora well and carry out the plugging work, despite the permanent injunction that had restricted access more than two decades ago.You use AI every day. articles.title: Are H-1Bs in trouble? Immigration experts on why Cognizant, Infosys, Microsoft are not getting timely approvals on job visas
articles.summary: Immigration attorney Emily Neumann said she has been seeing multiple cases of H-1B petitions from three tech giants not getting approved on time.
articles.body: Immigration attorney Emily Neumann said she has been seeing multiple cases of H-1B petitions from three tech giants not getting approved on time. Neumann said Cognizant, Infosys, and Microsoft at the moment are experiencing H-1B issues but she was certain that it would continue and would spread to other companies as well -- and it was not just a coincidence.Neumann said all these three companies are the highest sponsors of H-1B visas and their H-1B extensions and H-1B transfers are stuck with USCIS. The government has not issued any clarification but it could be tied to past layoffs; ongoing extensions into the alleged H-1B fraud. "The USCIS, the DHS, the DOL all have tiplines to report H-1B fraud, and this delay could be tied to any investigation. I would expect it to continue and spread to other companies," Neumann said.Immigration attorney Rahul Reddy said the Donald Trump administration does not want the H-1B visa program and it is clear. Vice President JD Vance, who is a top speculative candidate for the presidential race in 2028, wants to end the H-1B visa program, Reddy said, adding that the top three tech companies seeing the H-1B petitions stuck sends out a clear message.Reddy and Neumann said first Cognizant faced the heat: they filed H-1B extensions, applied for premium processing but the approvals did not come on time and now Infosys and Microsoft are seeing the same issue.Major H-1B crackdown in 2026 so far H-1B lottery is no longer purely random; it is wage-based.$100,000 H-1B fee has become a major legal battle, though it is blocked by the court. The Trump administration extended the fee for another year.DHS has proposed a permanent $103,265 H-1B fee, separate from the contentious $100K fee. The proposal was published in August and would apply to cap-subject H-1B petitions.More scrutiny for companies that have laid off US workers: A September 18 executive order directed the Departments of Labor, Homeland Security and State to consider whether an H-1B sponsoring employer has recently laid off, or plans to lay off, similarly situated US workers.JD Vance's White House fraud task force is targeting H-1B abuse: Vice President JD Vance is chair of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, created by President Donald Trump in March 2026. articles.title: India’s first high-altitude snow leopard safari flagged off in Ladakh
articles.summary: LEH/JAMMU: Ladakh lieutenant governor, Vinai Kumar Saxena, Wednesday flagged off India’s first high-altitude wildlife safari focused on snow leopard
articles.body: LEH/JAMMU: Ladakh lieutenant governor, Vinai Kumar Saxena, Wednesday flagged off India’s first high-altitude wildlife safari focused on snow leopard trails, with an aim of making local communities “equal partners in protecting and promoting Ladakh’s wildlife and benefiting economically”.“Wildlife should not be protected at the cost of people, nor should development come at the cost of wildlife. We must create a model in which both can thrive together,” the LG said after flagging off six safari vehicles.The project, operated by the Snow Leopard and High-Altitude Nature Conservation (SHAN) Society in collaboration with the UT’s forest department, has mapped the safari routes through Hemis National Park, Changthang and Karakoram Wildlife Sanctuary, besides Nubra, Zanskar, Sham, Kargil, and Drass districts.Ladakh has 477 snow leopards out of 477 across India. The region is also home to more than 38 mammal species, over 340 bird species, and around 1,800 vascular plant species.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Christa Pike feeling 'angry and confused' after waking up in the hospital following failed execution, her lawyers say
articles.summary: "Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," her legal team said in a statement.
articles.body:
Christa Pike is feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital in the wake of a failed execution attempt that left her with severe physical health challenges that put her on a "long road to recovery," her attorneys said on Wednesday.

Pike had been unconscious and in critical condition in the days after two doses of pentobarbital failed to end her life on Sept. 30, they said.

"On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain-dead and that life support would be removed the next day," Randy Spivey, a member of her legal team, said during a press conference Wednesday afternoon. "But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking."

Spivey said the effects of the pentobarbital have caused her to develop a blood clot, pneumonia and left her arms and hands "tremendously swollen," to the point where she's not currently able to use them. He added that Pike is still dealing with significant "cognitive confusion," but is "very aware" that the state had tried and failed to end her life.

The press conference came shortly after a hearing in which a judge granted Pike's attorneys' request to order the state to preserve all evidence connected to the execution, including medical equipment, communications related to the decision to call off the procedure or related to her emergency care and "anything that was in the actual room." The judge also ordered that any "barriers" that may prevent Pike from communicating with her attorneys while she's in the hospital be removed.

Pike's lawyers have repeatedly asked for Pike's death sentence to be commuted. During Wednesday's hearing, a lawyer representing the state declined to answer when asked whether Tennessee might attempt to execute Pike for a second time in the future.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press on Tuesday that Pike's regaining consciousness "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health won't be clear for some time.

"She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here."

Fallout from the failed execution has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and announced that the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, would be stepping down at the end of October.

Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement, according to ABC News.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was scheduled to be carried out after 30 years on death row, but was called off after the drugs she was administered did not kill her. She was taken to the hospital, where she received life-saving care.

Both of Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived at the hospital, her lawyers wrote in a legal filing. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream.

"It was cruel, and it was torturous," attorney Randy Spivey said the day after the execution attempt. "It was also predictable."

Spivey said Pike's legal team warned the state of Tennessee and the courts that her medical condition of thrombocytosis "would cause her to suffer an agonizing death." They said it could increase clotting and pain during the execution process and that her veins are difficult to access. Pike's attorneys said the state and the court dismissed their client's concerns.

In audio recordings obtained by the New York Times , Pike had said two weeks before she was due to be executed that she was concerned about the lethal injection, citing a recent botched execution attempt in Tennessee of Tony Carruthers in May, when staff were unable to locate a vein. "Tony Carruthers lived out my worst nightmare," Pike can be heard saying in the audio, which was shared by her lawyers.

"I do not have good veins,' she said. "And I don't want to go through that."

"She was not seeking to delay her execution," attorney Stephen Ferrell told reporters on Oct. 1. "She was seeking to have that execution performed humanely and as quickly and as painlessly as possible."

Following the failed execution, Lee ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and said that another execution scheduled for Dec. 3 later this year had been paused.

"This is a tragedy," he said. "There is no one who wanted what happened last night to happen. It's deeply disturbing to me that this has happened in this state."

Pike's attorneys said in response that the governor's independent review doesn't go far enough after being in solitary confinement for more than 20 years and the botched execution attempt. "Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty," Spivey said. "The governor must commute Christa's sentence now.

May Martinez, the mother of Pike's victim, Colleen Slemmer, told NBC News the execution attempt had been a "mess," adding, "They didn't say anything, and then, all of a sudden, they asked all the victims to leave. We didn't know anything until we got up to the office and saw the commissioner. And he said that it didn't work ... and she's on her way to the hospital."

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, said Tennessee should look at other forms of execution. "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully," she told The Associated Press.

Tennessee officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, or explained what went wrong.

Her condition could complicate any future attempt. Under Supreme Court precedent, a person can't be executed unless they have a "rational understanding" of why they are being put to death, the New York Times reported . Dr. Joel Zivot, an Emory University anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defense team, told the BBC it is "very possible" she suffered a brain injury because resuscitation was delayed.

Pike's lawyers have asked Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison. Lee had denied her clemency before the execution attempt.

President Trump questioned how the execution could have failed, telling reporters it "shouldn't be very difficult," according to AFP . United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk urged Tennessee not to try again.

What happened during the execution attempt?

Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for killing Slemmer in 1995, at the age of 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, a stay that was subsequently overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Media witnesses said officials raised the curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.

However, Pike remained conscious after the first dose. Nashville Banner reporter Steven Hale said she lifted her head off the gurney at 7:54 p.m. She also reportedly asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way.

Tori Gessner, a journalist with WKRN News 2 in Nashville, said Pike was seen pointing at her arm and asking, "Does this happen like that?"

By 8:26 p.m., witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement was made to escort media witnesses out of the area.

Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper on Wednesday night, "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced was "singular and unparalleled."

Seven other people have survived medical problems caused by an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.

"I've witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee," Gessner said. "Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg."

A source told NBC News that there was no medical oxygen or mask in the execution chamber, meaning they had to be brought in from a prison clinic. Some of the medication had worn off by the third time staff checked on Pike, the source added.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office."

The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not specify what happens if the subject is still alive after the second set.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and that the execution was violating her right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit and a district court.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 after being convicted of first-degree murder of Colleen Slemmer the previous year on the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.

According to legal documents filed with the Supreme Court , Pike "tortured, and killed Colleen Slemmer" on Jan. 12, 1995 because Pike "just felt mean that day." Pike is reported to have cut Colleen's throat multiple times and crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.

Pike was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder after trying to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones in 2001.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), there were 75 botched lethal injections between 1982 and 2010. Compared to other methods, lethal injections face complications at a significantly higher rate. There have been a number of botched executions since 2010 that don't appear in the DPIC's tally.

Most of these were executions that went wrong in some way, but still ended in death. But there are seven known instances in which an execution failed entirely. One of them was earlier this year in Tennessee, when staff were unable to find a vein to administer the lethal drugs to inmate Tony Carruthers.

More than 20 pharmaceutical companies have also refused to have their products used in executions, which has left states struggling to find the drugs they need to perform lethal injections. In some cases, they have experimented with unproven alternatives, with disastrous results.

An Oklahoma prisoner named Michael Lee Wilson said he could feel his "whole body burning" as he was being executed using a controversial drug cocktail in 2014. There have also been instances of prisoners gasping for air , heaving and coughing , convulsing and being subjected to "three hours of pain" before finally dying.

In April 2022, Tennessee called off the execution of Oscar Smith about an hour before it was scheduled to begin after the state discovered that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. An independent investigation found that the state had repeatedly failed to follow its own drug-testing protocols between 2018 and 2022.

Tennessee then revised its protocol, resuming executions in May 2025 and using a single, lethal drug: pentobarbital.

There's also growing evidence that lethal injection may not provide a peaceful death even when everything appears to go right.

Difficulties with lethal injections have led some states to revive previously discarded execution methods. South Carolina carried out three executions by firing squad last year. There had been three total firing squad executions in the U.S. in the previous half-century combined.

There were 47 executions in 2025 , according to the DPIC, higher than the recent average of fewer than 30 per year. These included the lethal injection of South Carolina inmate Marion Bowman , who received twice the intended drug dose, and Tennessee inmate Byron Black , who reportedly showed sustained cardiac activity for nearly two minutes after prison staff pronounced him dead.

articles.title: Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi detained over election chief protest
articles.summary: Rahul Gandhi has been arrested several times at protests demanding the resignation of poll body chief.
articles.body:
Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has been detained for the third time in two days during a protest demanding the resignation of the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.

Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were apprehended by police on Wednesday as they marched towards Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in India’s capital, New Delhi.

A live feed on the YouTube channel of Gandhi’s Congress Party showed police taking him into a vehicle and driving away. Authorities also detained several other opposition lawmakers and protesters.

Opposition parties, their student units and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing the poll body he heads of benefiting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

India’s Election Commission has so far removed more than 130 million names from the voter lists, with millions appealing the removals. About 969 million people were eligible to vote in the 2024 election.

Protesters allege the changes disproportionately removed voters who support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters more likely to back Modi’s party.

The commission and government deny the allegations. They say the revision has no political motive but is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring eligible voters remain registered.

Opposition lawmakers led by Gandhi protested on Tuesday as well, before police broke up their gathering and ‌‌ briefly detained them .

Speaking before his detention on Wednesday, Gandhi said protesters showed up unannounced after Delhi police “stopped” their gathering the day before.

“We will go to the designated protest site, sit there, and tell the country that, for us, Gyanesh Kumar is not the legitimate commissioner,” he told reporters, referring to Jantar Mantar.

“The people who have done this [vote theft] are traitors … Gyanesh Kumar will have to resign,” he ⁠⁠added.

There was no immediate comment from the police on the detentions.

The demonstrations present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party ‌‌youth ‌‌movement forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.

The “Cockroach” protests, one of the most visible signs of public dissent against Modi’s government in recent years, reflected growing anger over job scarcity, corruption and a lack of government accountability.

articles.title: ¡Lindsey Vonn podría volver a la Copa del Mundo con 41 años y tras casi perder la pierna izquierda!
articles.standfirst: Está inscrita en el equipo estadounidense para la próxima temporada, que empieza en dos semanas
articles.summary: Está inscrita en el equipo estadounidense para la próxima temporada, que empieza en dos semanas
articles.body: Lindsey Vonn, una de las más grandes figuras de toda la historia del esquí alpino, acaba de ser inscrita, de forma sorprendente, como una de las integrantes del equipo de élite de los Estados Unidos que disputará la Copa del Mundo de ese deporte, que arranca dentro de dos semanas y media en el glaciar austriaco de Sölden (Tirol). Vonn, de 41 años, campeona olímpica y doble oro mundial -suma hasta once medallas en grandes eventos-, es cuádruple ganadora de la general de la Copa del Mundo, competición en la que atesora 84 victorias, la tercera mejor marca de todos los tiempos tras su compatriota Mikaela Shiffrin (110) y el sueco Ingemar Stenmark (86). En los pasados Juegos de Milan-Cortina d'Ampezzo (Italia), en febrero de 2026, sufrió un aparatoso accidente en el descenso olímpico disputado en la citada estación de los Dolomitas que le provocó una compleja fractura de la tibia izquierda. Tanto que estuvo a punto de costarle la amputación de la pierna y por la que tuvo que ser operada en varias ocasiones. Lindsey, la reina histórica del descenso -con ocho Bolas de Cristal en esa disciplina, en la que cuenta 48 victorias en Copa del Mundo- acaba de ser incluida en el equipo A de la Federación Estadounidense de Esquí que participará en la competición de la regularidad, que integran un total de 17 esquiadoras y esquiadores; y en la que la legendaria campeona podría competir, cuando esté recuperada del todo, gracias a una invitación ('wild card'). La estrella de Saint Paul (Minnesota), que ya había sorprendido al regresar casi seis años después de su retirada -en los mundiales de Are (Suecia) de 2019- a la alta competición, con una rodilla de titanio -la derecha-, rizó aún más el rizo la pasada temporada, cuando se anotó los descensos de la Copa del Mundo disputados en St. Moritz (Suiza) y Altenmarkt (Austria). A pesar de haberse roto el ligamento cruzado anterior de la 'otra' rodilla, la izquierda, debido a una grave caída en el descenso de Copa del Mundo de Crans-Montana (Suiza), el pasado 30 de enero y el último antes de los Juegos, Vonn -Premio Princesa de Asturias de los Deportes en 2019- anunció siete días después que iba a competir en la prueba reina del deporte rey en la cita olímpica invernal de Cortina d'Ampezzo. Demostrando un enorme arrojo, Lindsey -que llegó a marcar el tercer tiempo en el segundo entrenamiento para la prueba- tomó la salida en el descenso olímpico. Pero se cayó tras un salto en la parte alta -en el primero de los cinco sectores- de la mítica pista Tofana, de la que tuvo que ser evacuada; protagonizando la imagen más triste de los pasados Juegos. El regreso inmediato de Vonn parece prácticamente descartado, ya que la esquiadora aún sufre las secuelas de esa caída. A finales de abril, la propia campeona había anunciado que no se produciría ninguna novedad antes de la temporada 2027-28. Para noviembre está prevista una nueva intervención quirúrgica en la que se le retirará el material metálico de la pierna y se le recompondrá el ligamento cruzado. "Una vez reparado el ligamento cruzado, el proceso requiere otros seis meses", había declarado Vonn en su momento. Esto, sobre el papel, descartaría también su participación en los Mundiales, que se disputarán del 1 al 14 de febrero próximos en Crans Montana (Suiza). Pero, de momento, la muy resiliente Lindsey figura entre los inscritos por la federación estadoundiense para competir en la Copa del Mundo. ¿Lo logrará? Veremos...

articles.title: Mike Waltz fights back tears revealing what Hamas hostage refused to do before release
articles.summary: Eliya Cohen, freed after 505 days in Hamas captivity, and Nova festival survivor Ziv Abud shared their harrowing stories at the United Nations.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS — Three years after the worst massacre in Israel’s history, Eliya Cohen — who survived 505 days in Hamas captivity — took the stage at the United Nations alongside his newlywed wife, Ziv Abud, a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre, and tried to explain to some of the world’s top diplomats what he had endured. "They didn't let me change clothes or to get a shower, even to eat or to drink," he said. "They chained me with heavy iron chains by my leg," Cohen said during an emotional discussion moderated by Dr. Phil McGraw at Israel’s U.N. commemoration Tuesday. He said lights were kept on to prevent the hostages from sleeping and that captors would enter repeatedly during the night screaming in an effort to frighten them. Cohen said they were not permitted to use a restroom and that at times survival felt almost impossible. FREED HOSTAGE ROM BRASLAVSKI DETAILS ABUSE, STARVATION DURING 738 DAYS IN GAZA CAPTIVITY But he described repeatedly forcing his mind away from the violence and toward the possibility of returning home. "Don't think about the violence. Don't think about the torture. Don't think about everything," Cohen recalled telling himself. "Just continue, stay strong. And maybe one day, you will come back home to your family." Cohen was among the 251 people abducted during the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when about 1,200 people were killed in southern Israel in their homes and at the Nova Music festival. It was the deadliest single day in Israel’s history. He personally lost 48 people he knew that day. His wife, Ziv, carried a different piece of the same story. Abud and Cohen had arrived at the Nova festival shortly before dawn with her 19-year-old nephew Amit and his girlfriend Karin. When the attack began, they eventually took refuge in a roadside bomb shelter that Cohen said was designed for roughly eight people but became packed with 29. HAMAS USED SEXUAL VIOLENCE 'DELIBERATELY AND SYSTEMATICALLY' ON OCT 7, COMMISSION REPORT FINDS Abud told the audience that more than 40 terrorists later attacked the shelter with grenades and gunfire. One man inside repeatedly grabbed grenades and threw them back outside before he was killed, she said. As the attack continued, Cohen covered Abud with bodies — an act that saved her life. "I lost my consciousness. Eliya was kidnapped," Abud said. "And after seven hours, I woke up in the shelter. I found myself in a pile of bodies." She paused, fighting back the tears. "It wasn't even bodies. It was body parts." Abud said she then saw that Amit and Karin had been killed. "I needed to sit with the bodies for seven more hours," she said. She was eventually rescued, one of seven survivors from the shelter. "We were four people that went to the festival from the same house," Abud said, "And I'm the only one that came back home that night." FORMER HAMAS HOSTAGE COUNTERS HASAN PIKER’S UT AUSTIN EVENT WITH HER STORY OF SURVIVAL For 505 days, she campaigned for Cohen’s return without knowing whether the man she loved would ever come home. Cohen, meanwhile, said he believed while in captivity that Abud had been killed. The couple married weeks before Tuesday’s ceremony. "But now he's here," Abud said. "And I can look forward to the future after we got married." She said she hoped the years ahead would include "kids and family because we are here and we survived. And we need to live a normal life," she said. Another Oct. 7 survivor who addressed the diplomats was Oriya Berlin, a young Israeli visual intelligence observer who had arrived at a base in the Gaza border area just two days before the attack. Berlin said she woke on the morning of Oct. 7 believing she was hearing a thunderstorm. "Outside, thousands of missiles were raining down with a single objective: to destroy my life and the lives of my friends," she said. Berlin and four other soldiers ran barefoot and in pajamas into a small shelter. They were unarmed. She said the women initially believed the incursion would resemble scenarios they had studied during training — a small squad that Israeli forces could quickly contain. Seconds later, she said, they heard vehicles and gunfire. Berlin described roughly 60 heavily armed terrorists attacking the base. At one point, she said, a message appeared in the unit’s WhatsApp group telling soldiers to shout "IDF" in Hebrew so Israeli troops could find them. The broken Hebrew immediately raised suspicions that a terrorist had taken a soldier’s phone. They remained silent. Berlin said they then heard another group shouting for soldiers to identify themselves, followed by a burst of gunfire and silence. Ten hours after the attack began, she said, special forces finally reached them. THE SENATE HAS REMEMBERED AMERICA’S OCTOBER 7TH VICTIMS. NOW IT’S TIME TO HEAL Berlin said that after learning how many of her friends had been murdered or kidnapped, she could not remain at home. Although she was offered the opportunity to leave military service, Berlin said she refused and returned as an observer for another six months before later moving into the IDF Public Diplomacy Office. "I wanted the world to see that the IDF is not just an intimidating military force on a television screen," she said. "It was also a 5'2" fake blonde girl like me who simply wanted to protect her home, her family, and her friends." She said she has since spoken before audiences ranging from international organizations to high school students who told her "I was wasting their time because of their deep-seated anti-Israel hostility." "But I stayed," Berlin said. "I spoke because the truth demands a voice." Berlin said her decision to continue speaking was rooted in the friends who did not survive. Before the ceremony, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz met privately with Cohen and Abud, asking Cohen how he was feeling physically and telling the couple how good it was to see them "healthy and alive." Minutes later, from the stage, Waltz became visibly emotional as he recounted a part of Cohen’s captivity that he said he had been unable to get out of his mind. Waltz said that on the night before Cohen’s release, Hamas tried to make him record a propaganda video claiming he had been treated well. "He refused," Waltz said. "He held firm. He said no." Waltz said Hamas again tried to turn Cohen’s release into propaganda the following day, placing him before cameras and instructing him to raise his hands. "He refused again," Waltz said. "Eliya, we salute you. I salute you," Waltz continued. "You are a proud, strong Jew. You're undefeated, man" he said with his voice breaking. The hostage crisis stretched over two years and several rounds of negotiations, releases and rescue operations. Waltz told Fox News Digital after Tuesday’s ceremony that he wanted the commemoration to acknowledge both the loss of Oct. 7 and how much had changed since. "Oct. 7, 2023, was their 9/11, was their Pearl Harbor," Waltz said. "More Jews were brutally massacred that day than any day since the Holocaust." ISRAELI OCTOBER 7 SURVIVORS CONQUER TRAUMA ALONGSIDE LEGENDARY ROCK ICONS IN POWERFUL NEW DOCUMENTARY He said it was important "to recognize the loss" and "hear directly from the survivors," but also to take stock of the region three years later. "We have President Trump's 20-point peace plan. We have a U.N. resolution establishing the International Stabilization Force," Waltz told Fox News Digital. "He's determined to not repeat what's happened so often in the past, where Hamas rebuilds, Iran rearms, they attack again, and you have this devastation all over again." Waltz pointed to broader shifts across the Middle East. "Iran is on its back foot. Lebanon has hope, Syria has hope. Iraq has hope," he said. He said he hoped the commemoration could combine "remembrance, the perspective, and I think charting, trying to chart a path of hope and peace for the future." From the stage, Waltz argued that Oct. 7 had produced the opposite strategic result from what Iran and its allies sought. "Oct. 7 completely, and I think irreversibly, has backfired on Iran and all of their terrorist proxies," he said, pointing to changes in Syria, Lebanon and Iraq and the expansion of Israel’s regional relationships. He ended with a message to the audience: "America will stand with the Jewish people." "Be strong. Be resilient. Be wise," Waltz said. "And know that what you're doing is right. Stand with your moral compass and know that this administration, the United States of America, stands with you." Israeli Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon used the gathering — attended by ambassadors and diplomats from multiple countries — to turn his attention to the institution hosting it. MOTHER OF OCTOBER 7 HOSTAGE WHO WAS EXECUTED UNPACKS HER GRIEF IN NEW MEMOIR "Even in this building, the U.N. is trying to demonize and isolate Israel," Danon said. "They have turned the victim into the accused, comparing our IDF soldiers to Hamas terrorists." Danon said he has been told by colleagues that he takes criticism of Israel at the U.N. ‘too personally’. "Indeed, it is personal," he responded. "My daughter is serving right now in the IDF. My son served as an officer in the IDF," Danon said. "He was supposed to be on the Re'im base next to Gaza on Oct. 7. The last minute, he was released home for the holiday." "That's why it's personal," Danon said. "The U.N. tries to demonize all of our sons and daughters, our lions and lionesses who give everything so we can freely live in our homeland. So yes, it is personal. It's personal for all of us." For Cohen and Abud, however, the event eventually returned from geopolitics to something much smaller: the possibility of an ordinary future. Abud said they hoped to have children and build a family despite knowing that Oct. 7 and the 505 days that followed would remain part of their lives. Cohen, asked by McGraw what he would say if the terrorists who abducted and tortured him were watching, needed only a few words. "I won," Cohen said. "I won and I'm here." He then turned his message outward. "Stay proud to be Jewish," Cohen said. "And stay proud to be Israeli." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are here to stay."

articles.title: Former Catholic bishop sentenced for abusing indigenous men in Australia
articles.summary: The Catholic Church in Australia has been marred by abuse allegations in recent years.
articles.body:
A former Roman Catholic bishop has been sentenced to six and a half years in prison for sexually abusing two young indigenous men in Western Australia.

Seventy-six year old Christopher Saunders was sentenced by the District Court of Western Australia and showed no reaction during Wednesday’s sentencing hearing.

In August, a court found Saunders guilty of one count of sexual penetration without consent and 12 counts of indecent assault.

The offences took place between 2010 and 2019 when he was bishop of Broome, a remote diocese in northwestern Australia.

Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, issued a statement apologising for the pain and suffering Saunders inflicted on victims, saying their trust had been “profoundly betrayed by a leader of the Church”.

Saunders was ordained a priest in 1976 and initially worked at mission stations in outback regions from the 1970s onwards. In the 1990s, he was appointed bishop of Broome by Pope John Paul II.

Following the abuse allegations, Saunders suspended his duties in 2020 and in August 2021 Pope Francis accepted his resignation. The clergyman has consistently denied the allegations.

It was revealed in court that the bishop had groomed his victims.

He is said to have regularly invited young indigenous Aboriginal men and teenagers to a beach house or a Catholic Church residence, providing them with alcohol and cigarettes, and giving them money and mobile phones.

The assaults on the two young men reportedly took place while they were heavily intoxicated.

In 2013, Australia’s government set up a Royal Commission , a high-level inquiry into institutional child sexual abuse, after a series of scandals involving the Catholic Church.

In 2017, the commission revealed that most of the abuse took place in churches, with seven percent of Catholic priests accused of abusing children in Australia between 1950 and 2010. It said allegations were almost never investigated.

It found that 4,444 alleged incidents of child sexual abuse had been reported to church authorities. In some dioceses, more than 15 percent of priests were perpetrators.

The commission also heard testimony from the Vatican’s former finance chief Cardinal George Pell, who was found guilty in 2018 of sexually abusing choirboys in Melbourne, Australia in the 1990s.

Pell – who had been Pope Francis’s anti-corruption tsar – was released from prison in 2020 after a court quashed his conviction. He died in Rome on January 10, 2023, at the age of 81 due to heart complications following hip surgery.

articles.title: Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims as Gaza lies in ruins three years on
articles.summary: Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attack that sparked the devastating Gaza war.
articles.body:
Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza .

Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage.

"The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day.

In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.

Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas-led attacks grapple with how to rebuild

Violence has continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed almost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.

On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023.

The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack.

Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid.

Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive.

Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose 21-year-old daughter Adi was shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the site was "dystopic, unimaginable" .

"Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12.

He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival.

Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killed in captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here."

Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.

Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened.

"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."

A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.

Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".

In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October.

"We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.

At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.

In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack .

The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.

Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.

They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.

Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.

The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.

Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement.

"They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."

Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture".

"We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you."

"The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.

Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."

She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well.

"That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.

This is the first anniversary of the 7 October attack with no hostages remaining in Gaza, but a US-brokered ceasefire deal from last year has failed to deliver peace or bring security.

There has been no end to Gaza's deadliest ever war, as Israel continues to carry out near-daily attacks.

More than 1,460 people have been killed there since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health ministry. The Israeli military says at least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in the strip over the same period.

Most of Gaza is in ruins, with nearly all the 2.1 million population still displaced amid dire humanitarian conditions.

An estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up and 1.2 million people living in tents or shelters, according to the UN.

Families who have been displaced several times during the war increasingly ask where they could go next, and whether they might even be forced to leave Gaza altogether.

Mohammed Emad al-Din, a 38-year-old father of two who works as a barber in Gaza City, said he had been displaced five times. His home was destroyed and his barber shop was partially damaged.

He told the BBC that the fear of being forced out of Gaza now follows him even into his dreams.

"I don't believe Israel caused all this destruction for nothing," he said.

"They have turned Gaza into a place that is almost impossible to live in, and I fear that we will eventually end up outside the place where we were born."

Another displaced Palestinian, Atta Saeed Hassan Shweikh, told the BBC that his son, daughter, sister and her children had all been killed during the war.

Speaking from Gaza City, he said Palestinians were "living in graves while still alive" and have endured "severe suffering".

At least three Palestinians were killed in Israeli strikes in the northern town of Beit Lahia and the southern city of Khan Younis on Wednesday, medics said.

The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas operatives in northern Gaza overnight, one of whom it accused of planting explosives near the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the territory still occupied by Israeli forces.

Hamas - which is proscribed as a terrorist organisation by Israel, the UK and others - released a statement praising the 7 October attack as a "historic milestone" in its "ongoing struggle project".

The statement, attributed to the group and disseminated in Palestinian media, called the attack "a natural response" to "bitter suffering" imposed by Israel.

articles.title: In 2018 or 2019, a thrift-store shopper paid just $1.50 for a purse because he thought it looked pretty; in a 2026 Antiques Roadshow episode, experts identified it as Cartier Art Deco and valued it at $35,000, with insurance above $100,000
articles.summary: A man who spent just $1.50 on a clutch bag at a thrift store discovered years later that his inexpensive find was actually a Cartier Art Deco piece valued
articles.body: A man who spent just $1.50 on a clutch bag at a thrift store discovered years later that his inexpensive find was actually a Cartier Art Deco piece valued at about $35,000.The unnamed buyer brought the bright orange velvet clutch to an episode of PBS's 'Antiques Roadshow', where it was examined by jewellery specialist Katherine Van Dell. He told her that he had bought the bag in either 2018 or 2019 simply because he liked the way it looked."I thought it was pretty," he said when asked why he had picked it up. At the time, there was little reason for him to think that the $1.50 purchase could be worth thousands of dollars.But Van Dell quickly noticed that the clutch was far from an ordinary thrift-store find. She described it as an "absolutely exquisite Art Deco purse" and began examining the decoration on its front flap. What initially looked like a colourful ornamental design was made from valuable materials and showed characteristics associated with fine jewellery from the Art Deco period.Precious stones reveal first cluesVan Dell explained that the decoration on the front of the purse was made using "carved rock crystal, rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and old European cut diamonds", along with platinum.The stones were arranged to resemble a small container filled with flowers. Van Dell described the design as "giardinetto", an Italian term meaning "little garden".Another important clue came from the way the small coloured stones had been carved and arranged. Van Dell identified the style as "tutti frutti", a design associated with colourful combinations of carved gemstones.While similar designs can also be seen in costume jewellery, Van Dell explained that the style was pioneered in fine jewellery by Cartier during the Art Deco period, although it was known by different names at the time.That raised the possibility that the purse could have been made by the French luxury jewellery house. The answer became clearer when Van Dell opened the clutch.Cartier name found inside clutchInside the bag, 'Cartier' was printed in gold on the lining. Van Dell said she suspected the piece was Cartier France.According to Antiques Roadshow, the clutch was likely made in the 1920s. The combination of its Art Deco design, precious stones, platinum construction and Cartier identification turned the thrift-store purchase into a much more valuable object than its owner had expected.Before hearing Van Dell's valuation, the buyer said he had hoped the purse might be worth $2,000 or $3,000. Even that would have represented a huge return on the $1.50 he had paid for it. The actual estimate was far higher."Conservatively in an auction situation today, it's worth about $35,000. And that's fair market value," Van Dell told him.The buyer appeared stunned by the figure and became emotional as he took in the appraisal. Van Dell praised his incredible eye for spotting the clutch at the thrift store in the first place.She also said the piece could carry a much higher figure for insurance purposes. According to Parade's account of the appraisal, Van Dell said the Cartier clutch could easily be insured for more than $100,000.The $35,000 surpriseThe difference between what the man paid and the appraisal was striking. A purchase made for just $1.50 because he found the bag attractive had turned out to be an Art Deco Cartier piece with a fair market value of about $35,000.The appraisal did not involve an auction sale, meaning the $35,000 figure was Van Dell's assessment of its fair market value rather than a price the owner had actually received for the clutch. The insurance figure was also separate from its estimated market value.The episode was filmed at Grant's Farm in St Louis, Missouri, and aired on May 11, 2026. The appraisal later drew attention online after Antiques Roadshow shared a video of the exchange, Parade Magazine reported. Viewers reacted to the buyer's emotional response after learning how much his thrift-store purchase could be worth.One viewer wrote, "He teared up knowing that $35k is life-changing for him. Wow." Others said they were happy for the buyer, with another commenter saying, "Looks like this happened to the right person."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Chinese runner dropped by sponsor after riding bike in marathon
articles.summary: Sun Yuanyuan was seemingly pictured on the back of another person's bike during part of the Berlin Marathon.
articles.body:
A Chinese fitness influencer has been dropped by her sponsor after she apologised for riding a bicycle during the Berlin marathon.

Sun Yuanyuan, known as Abeeeer on Chinese social media, had claimed a personal best during the event which was held in September.

But an Instagram page dedicated to monitoring inaccurate or misleading race times posted by influencers published a picture which appeared to show Sun on a bicycle between the 35km and and 40km marks.

Sun apologised and admitted to "breaking the rules". Brooks, the running shoe company, has ended its sponsorship deal with her and her finish time has been disqualified by the marathon organisers.

An Instagram account calling itself the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) posted a photo of Sun apparently on the back of a bike being ridden by another person during the marathon.

The page also posted a grid of Sun's "splits" - which are the times taken to complete different 5km segments of the race.

The grid appears to show that she sped up between the 35 and 40km marks, when she was allegedly on the bike.

Sun posted an apology on the Chinese social media platform Rednote, which was shared by OMTIU, admitting that she had broken the rules.

She wrote: "I won't make any excuses for this behaviour.

"I was feeling physically unwell on the course, [but] that is absolutely not an excuse for breaking the rules.

"My attempt to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the fairness of the competition and the spirit of the marathon."

Sun, who has 520,000 followers on Rednote, also said she "deliberately concealed" her actions, adding: "I feel deeply guilty about this."

Brooks confirmed to BBC News that it had dropped Sun.

A company statement said: "Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition.

"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual and publicly addressed the matter."

OMTIU was set up to highlight "the growing trend of GPS-based fabrication, selective Strava displays and false PR claims" among marathon runners, particularly fitness influencers. Strava is a fitness tracking app.

The page's mission statement says: "We exist to protect the integrity of the sport by ensuring that the times athletes share publicly reflect the times they actually ran."

Its Instagram bio describes it as "satire".

BBC News has contacted the Berlin Marathon for comment.

articles.title: 'One student, one day': CUET-UG 2027 may get shorter, simpler
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: CUET-UG 2027 could see some of its biggest changes yet - fewer subjects, shorter papers and a new grouping system aimed at ensuring that a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CUET-UG 2027 could see some of its biggest changes yet - fewer subjects, shorter papers and a new grouping system aimed at ensuring that a student can finish the entire entrance test in a single day instead of making repeated trips to examination centres.The ministry of education, University Grants Commission and National Testing Agency are working on a formula to shorten the overall examination cycle and simplify the experience for candidates, sources said.At present, a candidate can take up to five subjects in CUET-UG, with each paper lasting 60 minutes.Under one proposal being examined, the duration of individual papers could be reduced so that even a student taking five subjects can complete all tests within about 180 to 200 minutes.CUET-UG also mulls reducing number of subjects from 5 to 4Another option under discussion is whether the maximum number of subjects should be reduced from five to four. Sources said senior officials of the education ministry, UGC and NTA recently discussed the proposed changes and asked officials to examine how the examination could be compressed without affecting university admission requirements.A key part of the plan is to create subject groups based on commonly chosen combinations. This would allow NTA to schedule related papers together and complete a candidate’s examination in one sitting or on the same day.For example, physics, chemistry and biology could form one group for those seeking admission to science programmes. General studies could be added as a fourth paper where universities give weightage to its score. The idea is to bu-ild these groups around eligibility rules followed by universities.For instance, a student seeking admission to physics (Hons) at DU could choose the relevant three-subject combination rather than taking papers not required for the course.Officials believe such grouping could reduce the number of examination days and make scheduling easier. It could also end the problem of students having to travel to examination centres on different days for different papers. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: In Dayton, Ohio, both parties face bitter political despondency
articles.summary: Dayton voters expressed deep skepticism toward Vivek Ramaswamy and Jon Husted, saying neither party delivers real change to struggling Ohio communities.
articles.body: Generally, on reporting trips, the job begins once I land on the ground, hence, "on the ground reporting." But in Dayton, Ohio, I got my first tidbit of information in the air, looking out of my plane’s window to a large farm field below with the giant words, "Trump 28," blasted onto it like a crop circle. It was a reminder that President Donald Trump won the Buckeye State by 11 points in 2024, and, yet, both the Senate and gubernatorial races here are proving uphill climbs for the GOP’s respective nominees — Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy — even with Democratic challengers in former Sen. Sherrod Brown and Dr. Amy Acton whose support feels rather tepid. I spoke with Michael in the Oregon District neighborhood, one of few in this beat-down city of empty storefronts still brimming with life. His attitude seemed to be something akin to a pox on both political parties’ houses. FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC UNITY, REPUBLICAN CROSSOVERS SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE "It doesn’t seem like either candidate is going to be good for anybody," the young man said regarding Ramaswamy and Amy Acton. "It doesn’t matter who you vote for. Either way, they’re not going to represent what the people actually want." When I asked Michael if there was a politician these days who did inspire him, his answer was Texas GOP Congressman Brandon Gill, a far more populist figure than either the technocratic Ramaswamy or the establishment Husted, the latter of whom Michael admitted to knowing almost nothing about. At Blind Bob’s, I met Miss Barbara — as the men there all dotingly called her — a woman in her 70s who has lived in Dayton her entire life. She regaled me with tales of the busy metropolis she remembers from the 1970s and 1980s. "I suppose it was sometime in the '90s that things started going downhill," she told me, citing the loss of GM factories. On the elections, Miss Barbara told me, "I’ll start paying attention soon. I try to keep an open mind," adding in an echo of Michael. "Not much seems to change either way." Just down the road, I found Bonnett’s Book Shop, opened in 1939 by the grandfather of its current owner, Kevin. Once the world’s largest retailers of back-issue magazines, the shop has been a neighborhood fixture for generations. I asked Kevin what he was looking for from his state and federal governments. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS "In the last few decades, there’s been a big push for small businesses," Kevin told Fox News Digital. "There’s been a lot of help for new small businesses. ... We’re not a new business, we don’t get much attention." "We don’t get much attention," seemed to be a running theme from almost all the Daytonites I spoke with this week, very much directed at both political parties. There is a strong case to be made that no state in the union has suffered more grievously from the economic upheavals of the 21st century, from global trade to increased challenges in farming, than Ohio, where the emptiness of small-city America feels just a little more empty. It breaks one’s heart to see the monumental architecture of past glory, as intricate in detail as it is overpowering in scale, brought low, often literally empty shells of a once mighty Midwestern city. Sam, who runs a convenience store in the shadow of the abandoned stone and brick towers, told Fox News Digital, "It just feels like more of the same from both parties. Nothing much gets done." Given the dim view that many Ohioans take of traditional politics, it seems little wonder that Trump has consistently carried the state with big numbers on a message of rebirth and growth that, while it sometimes delivers less than it promises, at least it promises something. TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS Right now, there is not much indication that either Ramaswamy or Husted have the populist magic in a bottle that has rocketed Trump to victory, which explains why the president was in nearby Vandalia last weekend for a rally. Hopeless is too strong a word for Dayton, Ohio, but tired and skeptical are not; tired of a tame politics that cannot fix the big problems like massive amounts of empty commercial property, and skeptical that anyone running today can change that. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Over the next month, as Miss Barbara starts paying more attention, the Ohio candidates who can breathe a little hope into the voters will fare best. But it can’t be with either party’s familiar bromides; rather, it must be done with new ideas.

The ‘legendary’ Beverly Hills mansion has had many owners since. Doris Day’s family lived in the mansion for several years before it passed to Michael Caine, who is now 92. Ricky Martin lived there from 2004 until 2006.Martin sold the house to Michael Smith, CEO of natural gas exporter Freeport LNG, and his wife, Iris, for $15 million in 2006.The Smiths kept it for close to two decades as one of several homes in their property portfolio. The couple also had a Malibu beachfront home that they purchased from Hard Rock Cafe founder Peter Morton for $110 million, according to The Real Deal.For sellers, the rich Hollywood history was part of the pitch. Privacy and picturesque views are some other perks. "This exceptional Beverly Hills estate offers an unmatched combination of privacy, history, and panoramic views, presenting a rare opportunity to own one of the area's most storied and breathtaking properties."From $75 million to $35 million in four monthsIn August 2025, the Smiths listed the property on the market, asking $75 million, which is almost five times what they had paid for.But despite the famous previous owners, buyers did not rush in. A few weeks later, the asking price fell to just under $50 million. Real estate agent Carl Gambino of the Gambino Group at Compass took over the listing.The revised figure still didn’t attract buyers. The listing lingered until December. A famous address and a fresh renovation were not enough to hold the first asking price.Finally, on December 30, the deal was closed. The buyer paid $35 million, which is about 47 per cent of the original asking price. A $40 million gap. It still sits roughly $20 million above what the Smiths paid in 2006, before any renovation costs are counted. From listing to closing, about four months passed. The identity of the buyer remains unknown, and the price and closing date are the only hard details so far.What the buyer getsThe six-bedroom main house was pitched as the best of both worlds in terms of extravagance and comfort, with living spaces that feel spacious and cosy at once."The grounds include a luxurious main residence, guest house, lighted tennis court with pavilion, separate children's playground and play court, and a dedicated security house—all surrounded by vast lawns, lush gardens, and mature landscaping," the description on the listing reads.The primary suite "features its own terrace with city and ocean views". It also has a private sitting room, two bathrooms with dressing areas, enormous closets, and an adjoining flex room described as "ideal for a nursery, massage room, office or additional wardrobe."A private home theatre with its own snack room and a large kitchen are some of the highlights.Beyond the main house, the parcel holds a guest house, a lighted tennis court with a pavilion, a separate children's playground and play court, and a dedicated security house. From there, "state-of-the-art home, perimeter, and grounds security systems" are monitored.The house is designed to take full advantage of the views. The pool gives a beautiful view of the ocean. "From the moment you arrive, the most striking feature is the panoramic views—stretching from Mid-Wilshire, over Santa Monica and the ocean, all the way up the coast to Malibu," the listing says."These sweeping vistas can be enjoyed from nearly every part of the estate, including all the primary rooms, patios, yards, and terraces. Even the pool is positioned to allow for ocean views while swimming." The property also has an orchard, herb and rose gardens, and a motor court that can hold up to 20 cars.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Group of 20 graduates rescued after being abducted in Nigeria
articles.summary: The group was kidnapped earlier this month while travelling for a community service programme
articles.body:
A group of 20 young people who were abducted in South-East Nigeria last week have been rescued, police say.

The graduates were kidnapped on 1 October while they were travelling for a national community service programme in the Abia and Akwa Ibom states in the south of the country.

They were rescued by the police with the assistance of other security agencies.

Police spokesman Ani Iniedu said in a statement on Wednesday the group were rescued at Amakohia Ubi in Imo State after a sustained search-and-rescue operation. The group are being looked after and have been taken for medical evaluation.

Bombs preventing rescue of kidnapped youths, Nigerian police say

The police, military and other security agencies conducted intelligence-led searches of forests and suspected hideouts, he said, but he did not say whether any ransom was paid or if any arrests had been made.

The group of young people were participating in the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC), which is a compulsory one-year community service programme for most Nigerian university graduates, where people are posted to different parts of the country.

The group were travelling in two buses travelling on a major highway from Ibadan in southwestern Oyo state to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states when gunmen attacked the vehicles.

The incident has reignited concerns over insecurity and kidnapping along roads in the South-East.

Before they were released, the father of one of the people who were abducted, Omotosho Adewale, told the BBC that the kidnappers had demanded a ransom of 50m naira ($37,680; £28,440), which he could not afford.

"There's no peace of mind. I've not eaten in three days," he said in between tears.

Kidnapping for ransom is a major security problem in Nigeria, involving criminal gangs and armed groups. The authorities have not released any information about the identity of the attackers.
