articles.title: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.summary: The new charges are expected to accuse Maduro and his wife of playing a role in the torture of Americans in Venezuelan prisons, US media reports.
articles.body:
Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported.

The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS.

US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny.

The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan ​which brought the charges.

Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports.

Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges.

Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York.

The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.

The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term.

Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups.

They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States".

Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.

He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.

articles.title: Viral video of Arizona cheerleader slammed to ground by police and punched draws national outcry
articles.summary: National civil rights attorneys are questioning the “level of force” Tempe police used after they watched the video involving Arizona State cheerleader Eryn Bonner.
articles.body: Nationally recognized civil rights attorneys are questioning the circumstances around the viral video of Eryn Bonner, an Arizona State University cheerleader, who’s seen appearing to be shoved, slammed to the ground and punched by Tempe, Arizona, police after she tried to stop them from arresting her boyfriend. Ben Crump, who has represented multiple families in civil rights cases, including those of Trayvon Martin and George Floyd, posted a copy of the video on social media and asked, “Did this encounter really warrant this level of force?!” He added that officers “must prioritize restraint and de-escalation whenever possible.” In a separate posting, Lee Merritt, who represented the family of slain jogger Ahmaud Arbery, included photos of bruises under Bonner’s eyes. He said the ongoing internal review of her arrest should “examine whether Bonner imposed an immediate threat” and “whether force against her was necessary.” The Maricopa County attorney declined to bring charges against Bonner, 21, over the July 19 confrontation. The city later charged her with disorderly conduct and interfering with/hindering police, both misdemeanors. Edited videos released by police show Bonner trying to stop bicycle patrol officers from arresting her boyfriend when an officer, telling her to “back up,” shoves her hard enough to send her flying a short distance backward and landing flat on the ground on her buttocks. She returns and approaches the officer, yelling, “You want to punch a bitch?” In the video, she is tackled and her body falls across one of the bicycles as officers begin to try to restrain her. During the scuffle, a loud smack is heard as the officer who shoved her appears to punch her in the face. The video then shows officers trying to turn her over and cuff her. While one officer is grabbing her arms, another helping constrain her puts his hand on her buttocks and appears to squeeze. When they have her cuffed, police move her to a curb and sit her on the ground. She yells at them and says, “You see my f---ing face?” adding later that the officer pushed her down and punched her in her face. Bonner has filed a sexual assault complaint with the police internal affairs unit, alleging the officer who arrested her groped her buttocks after she was on the ground, contact that was captured on the video released by police. Bonner’s attorney, Benjamin Taylor, said that the misdemeanor charges were filed after Bonner filed her sexual assault complaint and that he believes the charges are retaliation and are intended to weaken her sexual assault complaint. “Why are they so vigilant in trying to charge a woman who is 21 years old and an ASU student?” Taylor asked. “Why are you trying to ruin her record for an incident where she was traumatized and trying to help her boyfriend?” The police department said the incident is still under investigation, and it provided previously released statements and video. It said that the city prosecutor’s office filed the charges “following careful review of the evidence” and that the decision to file charges was “not made in response to outside influences or any allegations regarding groping.” The police department said the timing of the city prosecutor’s charges was due to the City Prosecutor’s Office’s “conducting a thorough review of all available evidence before submitting charges.” Another video provided by police shows the moments leading up to the encounter. It shows Bonner and her friends walking past a man holding pizza boxes outside a business. There appears to be some conversation between one of the men with Bonner and the man holding the pizza boxes. Moments after Bonner and her friends walk away, one of the men with Bonner suddenly turns back toward the man with the pizza boxes and knocks them from his hand as the man identified as Bonner’s boyfriend tries to pull his friend back and away from the man with the pizza boxes. In moments, the bicycle patrol officers are intervening and tackling the men with Bonner as she yells at them to stop. Taylor, Bonner’s attorney, said the police should have first tried to de-escalate the incident. “There was no need for the officers to start tackling and throwing people down and start arresting people,” Taylor said. “They could have easily come up and talked to Eryn and her friends to figure out what’s going on.” Taylor said Bonner is an excellent senior student at ASU. She is a member of the ASU Sun Devils stunt and cheer team. Records show four speeding tickets and a cellphone-use-while-driving violation. All are closed. The video provided by police shows officers initially telling Bonner to back up as they move her aside. When they tackle her, she tries to pull her arms out of their grip before she is punched in the face. Police and the city of Tempe said in a joint statement Aug. 5 that the police department “takes every allegation of police misconduct seriously” because maintaining community trust depends on it. “Our officers are held to high professional standards and our community deserves confidence that allegations of this nature will be reviewed fairly, impartially and with great care,” they said. Taylor questions whether that is happening and is calling for the removal of Sgt. Kevin Ameiss, who contacted Bonner and told her he was leading the police internal affairs investigation. Ameiss had been suspended after an officer under his supervision held a Black hotel employee at gunpoint while seeking a white male suspect, according to a media report at the time. Taylor has also asked the mayor and the City Council to remove the investigation from the police department and have it conducted by a third party or another agency. “This assignment presents an egregious conflict of interest and severely undermines public trust in the Tempe Police Department’s accountability processes,” he said in his email to the city officials. Police said in a statement that Ameiss is part of a team led by a police lieutenant who has oversight of the investigation. They defended the probe as involving multiple layers of review and input, including potential use-of-force experts. Bonner faces a Nov. 4 hearing on the misdemeanor charges.

articles.title: Centre cites Supreme Court order, seeks to void Jharkhand DGP appointment
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Wednesday agreed to hear an application by Centre seeking the annulment of the appointment of Tadasha Mishra as Jharkhand DGP
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Wednesday agreed to hear an application by Centre seeking the annulment of the appointment of Tadasha Mishra as Jharkhand DGP on the ground that it was in violation of procedures laid down in SC's 2006 Prakash Singh judgement.Arguing that the appointments of the last two DGPs were also illegal, Centre said Mishra was appointed the state's police chief just a day before she was to retire, which was in conflict with the SC order that disapproved the practice among states to appoint DGPs on the last date of their tenure so that the person remained in the crucial position for two more years.SC had also clarified that the officers who are empanelled by the state, as far as practicable, must have two years of service left. Solicitor general Tushar Mehta said though an application on the matter was filed more than a month ago, it had not yet been listed for hearing. A bench headed by CJI Surya Kant directed it to be listed for Thursday.Centre questioned the legality of Jharkhand's 'Selection and Appointment of DGP (Head of Police Force) Regulation, 2025 and said the regulations are ex-facie violative of various SC directives, especially its ruling that a state could pick DGP from among those on a panel prepared by UPSC.A petition challenging the validity of the 2025 regulations was transferred from Jharkhand HC to SC in Aug last year. Jharkhand govt appointed Mishra as DGP on Dec 30 last year after amending its own 2025 regulations, which too mandated six months residual service prior to superannuation. MHA had written to Jharkhand to cancel the appointment and take steps to appoint a new DGP.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: MIKE EMANUEL: I joined an unknown startup called Fox News. It gave me a front-row seat to history
articles.summary: Mike Emanuel reflects on nearly 30 years of covering war, elections, and breaking news, from George W. Bush's Texas campaigns to the anchor chair.
articles.body: I was hired at Fox News in the first year of its existence — 1997 — before the vast majority of America knew what it was. In fact, I was hired without a job interview. The network’s top executives at the time offered me a job as a correspondent based on my audition reel. It was an odd feeling to go to work for people I had never met, at a network I had never seen. My career manager told me there were smart people at Fox who would likely figure out how to make it a success. So, I jumped at the chance to join the startup network. LAUREN GREEN: I WAS FOX NEWS CHANNEL'S FIRST ON-AIR HIRE. HERE'S HOW A DREAM BECAME A POWERHOUSE At that point, we were not available on cable TV in much of America. So, when I would call people about doing an interview for a story, they would ask if I was at the local Fox affiliate. Then they would ask where they could see Fox News. I told them we were working on it. But if they agreed to do a story with me, I would send them a VHS tape after it aired. About a month after I started, I was sent to London to work alongside the Fox team covering the death of Princess Diana. I thought that was going to be the story of my career. To be clear, it was a global story, but it was just the start of a truly extraordinary journey covering major national and international news of our time. JENNIFER GRIFFIN: I COVERED WARS, TERROR AND TRAGEDY FOR FOX NEWS. WHAT I FOUND WAS A FAMILY Evidently my Princess Diana coverage was decent. When I returned to our bureau in Los Angeles, my boss essentially interviewed me about where I had worked before local news in Los Angeles. I told him I was at the Fox station in Austin, Texas, covering politics. His ears perked up and he asked me if I knew then-Gov. George W. Bush. I told him the governor had nicknamed me "Mikey" since I covered his first campaign for governor in 1994 and his first couple of years in office. So, he asked if I could get a sit-down interview with Mr. Bush and instructed me to make it happen. After the governor did a couple of interviews with me in 1997, my bosses asked me to move to Dallas to open a bureau there to cover that whole region of the country. But the message was that if there was a Texas political story, they wanted me there to cover it. JIMMY FAILLA: I CAME TO FOX WITH MY TAXI DOUBLE-PARKED. THEN CAME THE RIDE OF MY LIFE I covered everything in that region and beyond from 1998 to just after President Bush’s 2001 inauguration. At one point, we were asked to come up with a story on a weekend because we needed more content for weekend shows. My team pitched going to the world’s largest rattlesnake roundup in Sweetwater, Texas. I think I nearly gave the folks in the control room in New York a stroke when I jumped into the pit with the rattlesnakes. I was wearing heavy boots and protective chaps, but the producers were scared to death I was going to end up in the hospital with snake bites. On election night 2000, I was on the platform in Austin, Texas, waiting to find out if George W. Bush had won or lost the election. We heard Vice President Gore had called to concede and then called back to say it was too close. Then for six weeks I camped out in Austin trying to figure out if Bush would be the 43rd president. Once that historic election was sorted out, my bosses asked me to move to Washington. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME When I arrived in D.C., I had no Washington experience, so my bosses used me to do all kinds of stories. When President Bush would return to his Crawford, Texas, ranch, they would send me since the president would typically call on me to ask a question if he saw me in the crowd of reporters. Six months after moving to Washington came Sept. 11, 2001. While the understandable focus of our coverage was on New York City, there was chaos in Washington, with concerns the White House and the U.S. Capitol could also be targets. My bosses sent me to the roof of our Washington bureau to do live updates on the situation here. From my position, we could see smoke behind me from the Pentagon. Later that day, I was doing reports at the Pentagon. A month later, I was sent to Islamabad, Pakistan, to cover the buildup to the war in Afghanistan. In early 2002, I was asked to go to Kabul to cover the war. Several of us went from being domestic correspondents to war correspondents virtually overnight. SANDRA SMITH: I WALKED INTO FOX NEWS 19 YEARS AGO. THE PEOPLE AND VIEWERS CHANGED MY LIFE Then in 2005, I was asked to embed with 10th Mountain Division soldiers who were tasked with securing western Baghdad so the Iraqis would be safe going to vote in an election. It was an amazing experience being with those brave men and women responsible for such a strategic location in the Iraqi capital. I had the opportunity to be a White House correspondent in the final years of President Bush’s term and the first years of President Obama’s presidency. Traveling across the country and around the globe with two American presidents was beyond my dreams when I started out in local news in Midland-Odessa, Texas, years ago. Asking questions of both presidents in the Oval Office and at presidential news conferences was also the honor of a lifetime. I had the opportunity to interview President Bush about being a wartime commander in chief and did the final TV interview with then-Vice President Dick Cheney. In 2011, Fox executives asked me to move to Capitol Hill to be the chief congressional correspondent, a beat I had never covered before in my career. There I covered a decade’s worth of State of the Union addresses, Supreme Court confirmations, Cabinet confirmations and my share of government shutdowns. While I covered Capitol Hill, network leadership started asking me to fill in as an anchor . I had confidence about doing it since for 20 years I had covered politics, war, natural disasters and more as a correspondent at the network. I felt like whatever news broke, I had probably covered it as a field correspondent before. I was grateful for the opportunity to fill in as an anchor on the network’s top news programs and became a regular anchor on weekends. While weekends are not typically as newsy as weekdays, massive stories break at any time. I was anchoring on Sunday, July 21, 2024, when then-President Joe Biden announced he was withdrawing from his reelection campaign. We were live and had the story first. We threw out the show rundown and went wall-to-wall for 90 minutes with the breaking news, totally unscripted. My producer Eric Strain would get in my ear to direct traffic. We would go from Kevin Corke reporting from the president’s weekend location in Delaware to Bret Baier on the phone to Brit Hume on the phone, back to Kevin, then to Martha MacCallum and Shannon Bream on the phone as the bosses rallied the weekday lineup to get into the office. At one point, Brit noted that this was history and congratulated me for being in the anchor chair to lead our coverage. I was also anchoring the weekend of June 21, 2025, when President Trump ordered Operation Midnight Hammer. That was a series of precision strikes on three major Iranian nuclear facilities. It was an opportunity for my experience reporting on Afghanistan and Iraq to help guide my questions from the anchor chair. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION And I was anchoring the weekend of January 3, 2026, when President Trump ordered Operation Absolute Resolve, a raid in Venezuela to capture Nicolás Maduro . We canceled our scheduled guests and went all in on the breaking news. It feels like there have been thousands of adrenaline-rush stories in my nearly 30 years at Fox News. My dream as a young journalist was to make it back to New York, so my parents, family and friends could watch me on the local news. I’ve lived far beyond those dreams. My loved ones have watched me cover major stories across the country and around the globe, and I will be eternally grateful for the opportunities my bosses have given me at Fox. articles.title: University of Arizona suspends fraternity activities as reports of misconduct persist
articles.summary: The University of Arizona has suspended activities at its fraternities following persistent reports of misconduct, including assault, hazing, and drug and alcohol-related behavior, a university official said.
articles.body: TUCSON, Ariz. — The University of Arizona has suspended activities at its fraternities following persistent reports of misconduct, including assault, hazing, and drug and alcohol-related behavior, a university official said. Just seven weeks into the fall semester, the university’s Dean of Students Office was investigating multiple misconduct reports involving nearly half the school’s Interfraternity Council chapters, Dean Chrissy Lieberman said Monday in a letter to the school’s fraternities and sororities announcing the suspension. The reports follow misconduct findings against some interfraternity chapters in the spring and multiple criminal investigations, according to the letter. “The number of cases under investigation and the severity of the concerns is egregious,” Lieberman wrote. University spokesman Nick Prevenas did not immediately respond to a request for more information about the criminal investigations on Wednesday. The Associated Press left messages with the university’s police agency. Officer Frank Magos, a spokesperson for the Tucson Police Department, said he was unaware of recent cases involving fraternities that were investigated by the city’s police agency. Prevenas also did not say whether the suspension was triggered by recent public outcry over how Cornell University handled allegations that multiple fraternity brothers sexually assaulted a woman in 2024. Lieberman’s letter noted that “the value of the Greek experience is under scrutiny nationwide.” The suspension prohibits fraternities from hosting, attending, participating in and sponsoring any organizational activities at least until their advisers have met with Lieberman at one of three meetings that were scheduled for Tuesday, Wednesday and Oct. 12, according to the letter. The letter said the dean’s office had reached “capacity” to investigate misconduct reports, and that reports continued even after the university’s president warned Interfraternity Council presidents at an August meeting about the possibility of additional consequences. “It is time for the University of Arizona Greek community to step up and set an example for good,” the letter said. “It is time to have difficult conversations with each other and the members of the community.” The university had previously suspended activities at the Sigma Tau Gamma fraternity after new members last year were reportedly forced to consume large quantities of alcohol and live goldfish and were subjected to screaming, degradation and threats, according to a Sept. 2 letter from a university official to the fraternity. An email and phone message at the fraternity’s national headquarters were not immediately returned. The AP also reached out to six other fraternity chapters at the University of Arizona’s campus via social media seeking comment on the suspensions.

articles.title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
articles.summary: British people need more incentives to invest in big firms listed in the UK, Dame Julia Hoggett, boss of the London Stock Exchange, says.
articles.body:
The UK needs to do more back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.

Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.

Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market , are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.

The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.

"If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss podcast .

The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion.

Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries.

But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange, travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York.

Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled.

Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.

It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns.

"We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said.

There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added.

But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said.

"We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit."

However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks.

She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks.

She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016.

Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange.

It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow.

The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month.

"As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said.
